Reporting violent crime in Japanese prefectures: specimen answer

Return to the exercise.

This document walks through a specimen answer to this exercise. Read each code section and its numbered explanations below. Select the number at the start of each explanation to highlight the line of code that explanation relates to.

In R, like in many programming languages, there is usually more than one way to complete a task. This code shows one way to complete this exercise. There are other ways to organise this code that are equally good and achieve the same result, but the code below tries to balance making the code efficient with making it easy to read. If your code is different from the code here, read through the notes below the answer and use those to decide whether you prefer your own approach or the specimen answer below. You can also use the notes to improve your own code.

WarningThe specimen answer expects your computer to be set up as outlined in the book.

The online textbook sets out how to install the software you need for crime mapping with R and set up your computer to store files in particular places. The specimen answer below assumes that you have followed those instructions and that your computer is set up as described in the book. If you have not done so, the code in the specimen answer may not run correctly.

Step 1: The YAML header

The first part of a Quarto document is the header, written in a format called YAML. This specifies a variety of document settings.

---
1title: "Violent crime in Japanese prefectures, 2012"
2author: "Joe Bloggs"
3date: today
date-format: "D MMMM YYYY"
4format:
  html:
5    embed-resources: true
6execute:
  echo: false
---
1
Specify a document title. A good title makes it easier for readers to understand what the report is about as soon as they open the document.
2
Specify the document author to help readers understand who produced a document and who they should contact with any questions they have. If you were completing this exercise for an assessment that was going to be marked anonymously, you should follow the assessment instructions to keep your submission anonymous.
3
Specify the date on which the report was produced, so that readers can make sure they are reading the most-recent version. The special value today tells Quarto to automatically insert today’s date. The date-format specifies the format that should be used for the date: D specifies that the date should show the day of the month without leading zeros, MMMM that it should show the full month name, and YYYY that it should show the year using four digits.
4
The format: header option specifies the file format that the report will be rendered into. This can either be a single value, such as format: html to produce a web page or format: docx to produce a Word document, or we can specify the format with additional options (as in the code here). In that case, html appears on the line after format:, html is indented by two spaces and is followed by a colon – that tells Quarto to look for additional options on the subsequent lines.
5
embed-resources: true is an option that is used only for HTML output. By default, web pages only include the text of the page itself, with items such as images (including maps and charts) stored in separate files. That makes it hard to move web pages around, so embed-resources: true tells Quarto to include all supporting resources in the HTML file itself. This makes it easier to share the report with others, because they only need the single HTML file to view the report.
6
The execute: options control how Quarto treats the code in the code chunks that follow. There are lots of options that we can specify here, but the only one we use in this case is echo: false. That tells Quarto that the R code in each code chunk should not be printed (‘echoed’, in coding jargon) in the final report. The code is still run, but it is hidden from the reader. This is important for this exercise, because the report is intended for a non-technical audience and they would be likely to find the R code confusing.

Step 2: Load packages

7```{r}
8#| label: setup
9#| output: false

# Load packages
10pacman::p_load(here, httr2, leaflet, sf, scales, tidyverse)
11```
7
To run R code in a Quarto document we need to tell Quarto that the code we have included is R code. We do that by surrounding the code with a code fence: for R code, the code fence is a line starting with ```{r}. Note that this code must appear at the start of the line – if there are any spaces or other characters before the code fence, Quarto will not recognise it.
8
Code fences contain a code chunk. At the start of a code chunk, we can specify different options to control how the chunk is run, where any output appears, etc. We specify these options in lines beginning #| (note the space after the | character). It’s almost always useful to specify a label for each chunk using #| label:, since when we render the complete document that chunk label will be used in any error messages (making errors much easier to find in long documents).
9
One thing we can specify at the start of a code chunk is how any output produced by the code should be displayed. It is important to do this to make sure that no raw R messages, warnings, etc. appear in our finished report, since a non-technical audience would probably be confused by that. For this chunk we don’t want any output to appear, so we specify output: false so that no output from this chunk is printed.
10
Inside the chunk we load all the packages we need for this script: here allows us to specify where to find files in the workspace; httr2 downloads data from the internet; leaflet creates interactive maps; sf handles spatial objects; scales formats numbers for including in text; tidyverse provides tools for reading, wrangling and plotting data.
11
We close each code chunk with the closing fence ```, which must also be at the very start of a line.

Step 3: Download the original data

```{r}
#| label: download-data
#| output: false

12# Download original crime and population data into the workspace
request(
  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/japan_violence_counts.rds"
) |>
13  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "japan_violence_counts.rds"))

# Download original prefecture boundaries into the workspace
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/japan_prefectures.gpkg") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "japan_prefectures.gpkg"))
```
12
request() specifies the URL of the file to download. The pipe operator (|>) passes that request to the next function. See Downloading and loading data; Stringing functions together.
13
req_perform() performs the download that was set up by request(). here() specifies where the original file should be saved, relative to the crime_mapping workspace. Keeping the original data in data/raw means we can return to it if we make a mistake while wrangling the data. See Keeping your files organised.

Step 4: Load and prepare the data

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| output: false

# Read crime and population data, removing the repeated prefix from measure
# names
14violence <- here("data", "raw", "japan_violence_counts.rds") |>
15  read_rds() |>
16  janitor::clean_names() |>
17  mutate(measure = str_remove(measure, "number of "))

# Read prefecture boundaries as spatial data, then transform to use longitude
# and latitude
prefectures <- here("data", "raw", "japan_prefectures.gpkg") |>
  read_sf() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
18  st_transform("EPSG:4326")
```
14
here() specifies the location of the downloaded file. <- stores the result of the whole pipeline as violence. See Keeping your files organised; Naming objects; Stringing functions together.
15
read_rds() from readr reads the data (.rds means the file is in R-data format).
16
janitor::clean_names() from janitor converts column names to snake_case. Using :: allows us to use this function without loading the whole package. See Cleaning column names; Loading packages.
17
If we were to look at the data we would see that most of the values in the measure column start with the fixed text “number of”. To make the data easier to wrangle later, we will remove the text at this point.
18
st_transform() transforms spatial data to use a coordinate reference system that is appropriate for the purpose we want to use it for. In the case of interactive web maps this needs to be “EPSG:4326”.

Step 5: Wrangle the data

The data provided for this exercise did not have a tidy data structure, so they need quite substantial wrangling before they can be used to calculate crime rates.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-rates
19#| output: false

20# Extract population from the raw data
prefecture_pop <- violence |>
  filter(measure == "population (thousands)") |>
  # Keep only the prefecture names and the population value, but change the name
  # to `pop` since `value` is ambiguous
  select(prefecture, pop = value) |>
  # Convert the population measure to number of people, since in the raw data it
  # is in thousands
  mutate(pop = pop * 1000)

21# Extract violence counts from the raw data
violence_counts <- violence |>
  filter(measure %in% c("violent crimes", "homicides", "robberies", "rapes")) |>
  # Rename the ambiguous `measure` and `value` columns
  rename(crime_type = measure, crimes = value)

# Join the data then calculate crime rates and ranks
22violence_rates <- prefectures |>
  # Select only the columns from the prefecture boundary data that we need, and
  # rename the column containing the English name for each prefecture
23  select(prefecture = adm1_en, geom) |>
  # Join violence counts to prefecture boundaries
24  left_join(violence_counts, by = join_by(prefecture == prefecture)) |>
  # Join population counts
25  left_join(prefecture_pop, by = join_by(prefecture == prefecture)) |>
  # Calculate an incidence rate
26  mutate(rate = crimes / pop * 100000) |>
  # Rank each prefecture for each type of crime (note that `.by = crime_type`
  # means the ranks are calculated separately for each crime type)
27  mutate(rank = min_rank(desc(rate)), .by = crime_type) |>
  mutate(
28    # Create a label describing the rate in each prefecture to be used in the
    # report *text*
    label = str_glue(
      "{prefecture} ({number(rate, accuracy = 0.1)} per 100,000)"
    ),
29    # Create a label to be used in the *maps*
    map_label = str_glue(
      "{prefecture}: {number(rate, accuracy = 0.1)} {crime_type} per 100,000 ",
      "residents (rank {ordinal(rank)} of {nrow(prefectures)})"
    )
  )
```
19
All the output from this chunk is stored in objects for later use, so we set output: false to make sure no stray output appears in the final report.
20
In the original data, some rows represent crime counts and some represent population counts. Subsequent wrangling steps are easier if the two types of data are stored in separate objects, so here we create an object containing only the rows of population data.
21
We now create a dataset that contains only the rows that contain crime counts. Note that we also rename some of the columns so that when we combine the data in the next step, we know which columns hold population counts and which columns hold crime counts.
22
Start a new pipeline based on the prefecture boundaries stored in the prefectures object. Starting with an object we know contains one row for each prefecture means that we will be able to identify if any of the other objects are missing values for some prefectures.
23
The prefectures dataset has many columns, so we keep only the column (adm1_en) containing the English language prefecture names, and rename that column to have a name that is easier to remember. At this point the result holds two columns: prefecture (the prefecture name) and geom (the boundary of the prefecture in SF format).
24
Add the violence counts from the violence_counts object. At this point the result holds four columns: prefecture and geom from the original prefectures object, and crime_type and crimes from the violence_counts object.
25
Add the population counts from the prefecture_pop object. At this point the result holds five columns: prefecture, geom, crime_type, crimes and pop, which is all the columns we need to calculate crime rates.
26
Use mutate() to calculate a rate of crimes per 100,000 people.
27
Use min_rank() to assign ranks for each prefecture for each type of crime. desc() means that the ranks will be assigned in descending order, i.e. the prefecture with the highest rate will be assigned the rank 1 and the prefecture with the lowest rate will be assigned the rank 47. .by = crime_type means that the ranks will be calculated separately for each value of the crime_type column in the data.
28
Use str_glue() to create a new column in the data that contains a text value that we can use in the report text to describe the crime rate in a particular prefecture.
29
Use str_glue() to create another new column containing a label that can be used on the maps in the report. This label is longer than the label to be used in the text because it specifies the rank along with the rate.

Step 6: Calculate summary values

It will be useful to use some summary statistics in the report text, and the code will be better organised if we calculate these all at once rather than separately each time we need a particular value.

```{r}
#| label: summary-statistics
#| output: false

# Calculate national rates from total counts and total population
national_rates <- violence_rates |>
30  st_drop_geometry() |>
31  summarise(rate = sum(crimes) / sum(pop) * 100000, .by = crime_type)

# Extract the five highest rates of overall violence into a vector in descending
# order, including any ties
high_five <- violence_rates |>
  # Keep only the overall violence rates
  filter(crime_type == "violent crimes") |>
  # Keep just the five prefectures with the highest rates
32  slice_max(order_by = rate, n = 5) |>
  # Extract the labels into a vector that we can include in the report text
33  pull("label")

# Select the highest and lowest rate prefecture for each individual crime type
highest <- violence_rates |>
  slice_max(order_by = rate, n = 1, by = crime_type)
lowest <- violence_rates |>
  slice_min(order_by = rate, n = 1, by = crime_type)
```
30
Before using summarise() on an SF object it is usually better to convert the data to a tibble by calling st_drop_geometry(), since this means summarise() runs much faster.
31
Calculate the national rate for each type of crime by taking the total of all the values in the crimes column (sum(crimes)) and dividing it by the total of all the rows in the pop column (sum(pop)). .by = crime_type specifies that this should be done separately for rows containing each unique value in the crime_type column, so we get a national rate for each crime type.
32
Use slice_max() to keep rows based on which 5 rows (n = 5) have the highest values in the rate column (order_by = rate).
33
Use pull() to extract only the label column from the result to produce a vector of values that we can use in the report text.

Step 7: Start writing the report text

This is the first part of the Quarto file that is not part of a code chunk. Since we have set output: false for all the code chunks above this point, that also means this will be the first content that appears in the report itself.

The Statistics Bureau of Japan supplies crime counts for Japan's `r nrow(prefectures)` prefectures. This report describes regional variation in recorded violent crime in 2012. It covers overall violent crime and separately homicides, robberies and rapes.

The code `r nrow(prefectures)` allows us to include R code within a paragraph of text in the report. Note that inline code such as this must start with `r (without a space between ` and r, but with a space after r) and end with `. It’s usually best to only put simple R code within text paragraphs like this – longer code is usually easier to read if it’s put in a code chunk (we will see some examples of this shortly).

Step 8: Write a section for each crime type

Note

In the code file (downloadable above) there is a code to produce a section of the report for each crime type. Since these sections each have the same structure, only the first section (for overall violent crime) is reproduced here.

The section for each crime type starts with an introductory paragraph of text. This includes both text and inline R code.

## Overall violent crime

The national rate of overall violent crime was `r number(pull(filter(national_rates, crime_type == "violent crimes"), "rate"), accuracy = 0.1)` recorded violent crimes per 100,000 residents. The five prefectures with the highest rates were `r high_five`, while the lowest was in `r pull(filter(lowest, crime_type == "violent crimes"), "label")`. @fig-overall-violence shows the distribution across all prefectures. Select a prefecture to read its rate, or move the pointer over it to show its label.

The code `r number(pull(filter(national_rates, crime_type == "violent crimes"), "rate"), accuracy = 0.1)` takes the national_rates object we created above, filters it to contain only the row for which crime_type == "violent crimes", extracts the rate column using pull() and then formats the rate into a human-readable number using number() from the scales package. The argument accuracy = 0.1 specifies that the rate should be rounded to one decimal place.

The code `r high_five` includes the value that we stored earlier in the high_five object, which is a vector of labels for the five prefectures with highest rates of overall violence.

The code `r pull(filter(lowest, crime_type == "violent crimes"), "label")` takes the lowest object we created before, filters it to contain only the row for which crime_type == "violent crimes" and then uses pull() to extract only the label column.

We now need another code chunk, this time to add the first interactive map to the report.

```{r}
34#| label: fig-overall-violence
35#| fig-cap: "Overall recorded violent crime per 100,000 residents in Japanese prefectures, 2012"
36#| out-width: "100%"

37# Extract just the overall violence rates
overall_rates <- filter(violence_rates, crime_type == "violent crimes")

38# Create a sequential palette with a fixed domain for this crime rate
overall_colours <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "Reds",
  domain = pull(overall_rates, "rate")
)

# Create the interactive map
39leaflet(overall_rates) |>
40  # Add a light base map
  addProviderTiles(
    "OpenStreetMap.Mapnik",
    options = providerTileOptions(opacity = 0.4)
  ) |>
41  # Colour prefectures by rate, with labels and click-to-open popups
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~ overall_colours(rate),
    fillOpacity = 0.75,
42    label = ~map_label,
    popup = ~map_label,
    weight = 1,
    color = "black"
  ) |>
43  # Give the rate units and year in the legend
  addLegend(
    pal = overall_colours,
    values = ~rate,
    title = htmltools::HTML("violent crimes<br>per 100,000<br>residents, 2012"),
    position = "bottomright"
  ) |>
44  # Acknowledge the statistical and boundary sources
  addControl(
    "Crime: Statistics Bureau of Japan (CC BY)<br>Boundaries: OCHA (CC BY-IGO)",
    position = "topright"
  )
```
34
This chunk produces a figure, which means we need to do a couple of things differently to the previous chunks. First, the chunk label must start with fig- so that Quarto understands it will produce a figure that we can refer to elsewhere in the report using (in this case) @fig-overall-violence. You can see we have already done that in the text above the figure. Quarto will automatically convert the cross-reference @fig-overall-violence into (in this case) the text ‘Figure 1’. Secondly, note that for this code chunk we have not set output: false because we want the output from the chunk (the map) to appear in the report.
35
We can use the #| fig-cap: chunk option to provide a caption that will (by default) appear just underneath the figure.
36
The #| out-width: "100%" chunk option specifies that we want the map to occupy the full width of the text column in the report. It is usually a good idea to make maps as big as reasonably possible so that readers can see a reasonable level of detail.
37
In creating the interactive map we will need to repeatedly use a version of the data that contains only the row relating to overall violence rates. Rather than filtering the data multiple times, we create a version of the data containing only the relevant rows here.
38
colorNumeric() creates a function that converts crime rates into colours. palette = "Reds" gives a sequential scale, with darker colours representing higher rates. domain = pull(overall_rates, "rate") specifies that the colour values should be based on the range of values in the rate column in the overall_rates object.
39
leaflet() creates a new, blank, interactive map using the prepared spatial data.
40
addProviderTiles() adds a base map to the blank map, using map tiles from OpenStreetMap. providerTileOptions(opacity = 0.4) makes the base map semi-transparent, making it less visually prominent so that the crime-data layer is the most prominent layer on the map.
41
addPolygons() adds the crime data to the map (with each prefecture being represented by a polygon). fillColor uses the overall_colours() palette function we created earlier; ~ tells leaflet to look up columns in the map’s data. fillOpacity = 0.75 lets the base map show through, and weight = 1 keeps outlines relatively thin.
42
label specifies the text (from the map_label column in the data) to display when a user hovers their mouse over a prefecture, while popup makes the same information available when a prefecture is clicked or tapped.
43
addLegend() uses the same palette and rate column. Wrapping the legend title in htmltools::HTML() allows us to use <br> to create a line break in its title.
44
addControl() adds the source acknowledgement as text on the map. Its first argument is the content to display, <br> separates its two lines, and position places it in the top-right corner away from the legend.
